Foreword

WHO launched the Strategic framework tropical diseases to advance a holistic,

Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) are among the most pressing public health challenges in the WHO South-East Asia Region. With 16 of the 21 recognized NTDs present, the Region bears a disproportionately high share of the global NTD burden—more than half of the global population requiring NTD interventions. According to 2024 data, the Region accounted for over 71% of all new leprosy cases globally, and over 64% of the worldwide population requiring mass drug administration for lymphatic filariasis. These statistics underscore the urgency of strengthening the Region’s health system readiness, particularly where most patients first seek care— the primary health care level.

Skin-related NTDs—such as leprosy, lymphatic filariasis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, and yaws—often present with visible manifestations that can lead to profound psychological distress, lifelong disability, and debilitating social stigma. Despite the severity of these impacts, many of these conditions are preventable and manageable. In 2022, for integrated control and management of skin-related neglected people-centred approach.

However, frontline health workers frequently encounter difficulties in recognising these diseases at an early stage, a challenge compounded by limited diagnostic capacity and constrained resources in remote or hard-to-reach communities. Early diagnosis, timely recognition of warning signs, and appropriate management can significantly reduce complications and help control transmission.

Glossary

Active case detection

This involves intensified initiatives to detect cases by screening for diseases within populations at risk. Active case detection is typically carried out outside of health-care facilities and considered active surveillance.

Active surveillance

The procedure involves actively identifying and reporting cases, with health authorities providing encouragement to health-care workers through individual contacts, feedback or other incentives. Community- based active case-detection activities may be conducted to increase the reported case numbers, often resulting in more comprehensive data, compared with passive surveillance.

Disability

Incapability to carry out regular daily tasks proficiently or autonomously; the adverse aspects of the interplay between an individual with a health condition and their surroundings, encompassing environmental and personal factors.

Integration

The bundling or “packaging” of multiple diseases, determined by their prevalence in countries, to streamline the collective implementation of interventions through a shared platform such as preventive chemotherapy and the utilization of multiplex diagnostics - this approach also includes integrated monitoring, evaluation and reporting for all pertinent neglected tropical diseases. Collaborative delivery is enhanced through integration among diverse health sectors.

Mass drug administration (MDA)

8.content:
This involves distribution of medicines to the entire population of a given administrative setting (for instance, state, region, province, district, subdistrict or village), irrespective of the presence of symptoms or infection; however, exclusion criteria may apply.

Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs)

A medically diverse set of bacterial, viral, parasitic, fungal and noncommunicable diseases and disease groups that disproportionately affect populations living in poverty, predominantly in tropical and subtropical areas - they remain a public health problem that affects populations left furthest behind by development in the most vulnerable countries and communities. They impose a devastating human, social and economic burden on more than one billion people worldwide.

Skin-related neglected tropical diseases (skin NTDs)

These refer to a subset of neglected tropical diseases with skin manifestations that impair, disable and disfigure, and may lead to stigmatization, discrimination and socioeconomic problems.

Stigma

A negative stereotype or perception that can lead someone to unfairly judge another person and falsely attribute negative characteristics to them, stigma can result in prejudice (negative attitudes) and discrimination (negative behaviour) against persons affected by skin NTDs and/or mental health conditions and their families.

vi

Total community treatment (TCT)

This involves a comprehensive approach aimed at treating the entire population residing in yaws- endemic communities. This strategy involves administering a single dose of azithromycin to all individuals, regardless of whether they are showing symptoms of yaws infection. A key component of the World Health Organization’s Yaws Eradication Programme, TCT is designed to interrupt the transmission of the disease within communities by treating both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals.

Total targeted treatment (TTT)

This involves providing yaws treatment for treating all individuals within a specific target group in yaws- endemic areas, typically focusing on groups with a higher likelihood of infection or transmission, such as school-aged children or individuals living in close proximity to known cases. This approach aims to achieve high treatment coverage within the target population to interrupt the transmission of the disease and prevent its soread. TTT may involve administration of antibiotics, such as azithromycin, to the entire target group, regardless of symptom status, as part of efforts to eliminate yaws.

Introduction

Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) are a diverse group of disease conditions that disproportionately affect populations living in poverty, particularly in remote and underserved areas. While their causes vary, including virus, bacteria, parasites, fungi and toxins, they share a common feature: all can result in serious health, social, and economic consequences. Many NTDs are preventable or treatable, yet they often receive less attention and fewer resources compared to other health conditions.

A number of NTDs present with visible manifestations on the skin, including diseases such as leprosy, yaws, lymphatic filariasis and scabies. Sharing this characteristic, these diseases are collectively referred to as “skin NTDs”.

To support countries in addressing these diseases more effectively, WHO launched the Strategic Framework for Integrated Control and Management of Skin NTDs in 2022. This approach aims to strengthen integrated strategies by promoting joint interventions, optimizing the use of available resources, and expanding access to care.'

Through the integration of skin NTDs services, it is anticipated that improved care will benefit not only individuals affected by skin NTDs, but also those with other skin-related conditions, contributing to the broader vision of “skin health for all”.

12.content:
Integrated approach to management of skin-related neglected tropical diseases and common skin conditions

Why so skin diseases - specifically, skin NTDs - matter?

Skin diseases may appear less serious Compared to other health conditions commonly encountered in your community, as they rarely result in death. However, breaks or wounds in the skin can lead to serious complications, including damage to internal organs such as the heart and kidneys. Because they are visible, skin conditions can significantly affect a person’s quality of life-causing psychological distress and limiting social participation. In the case of skin NTDs, complications resulting in visible changes or disabilities can be severe and, if not diagnosed and managed early, may lead to long-term or lifelong consequences.

Fortunately, skin diseases are often visible to the eye when present. This provides an important opportunity to recognize the condition and initiate treatment early-an essential step toward achieving effective outcomes.

Chapter 1

Skin lesion is an abnormal change of the skin, which distinguishes itself from the surrounding skin. Recognizing, analysing and properly understanding skin lesions are the entry point to making dermatological diagnoses. This chapter covers the flow of patient examination for skin conditions, followed by pictorial descriptions of different skin signs that are discussed in this booklet. Lastly, the algorithms for diagnosing the skin diseases that are commonly seen in the South-East Asia Region are provided.

1.1.1. How did it start? (ask/history)

The onset of a skin condition can generally be categorized as either “acute” and “chronic”. Asking patients when their symptoms began can assist in differentiating between various types of diseases. Acute conditions develop rapidly and typically last for a short duration, usually a few days to less than 4 - 6 weeks. They are often characterized by redness, pain, swelling, and warmth. Many bacterial infections, for example, cellulitis, are classified as acute conditions. Skin reactions due to external factors, for example, contact dermatitis, may also have an acute onset.

In contrast, chronic conditions progress gradually and may persist or worsen over an extended period, ranging from several months to years. These include a wide spectrum of conditions, from long-standing infections to diseases associated with daily habits or environmental exposures. The likelihood of developing chronic skin conditions tends to increase with age.

Sometimes, there are conditions that are between acute and chronic, and referred to as subacute. Subacute conditions are a vaguely defined state, described as somewhat or moderately rapid change. However, it usually refers to conditions that show change over a few weeks to a few months.

Also, asking the patient about any possible trigger or exposure that may have contributed to developing the disease can provide clues to making a diagnosis. For example, family history is an important piece of information for suspecting diseases such as scabies and leprosy.

Itchiness or pain can often help in differentiating between various skin diseases. For example, allergic reactions (eczema, atopic dermatitis, drug eruptions, etc.) are often itchy. To understand the different types of skin lesions, it is essential to first understand the structure of normal skin. In this section, we discuss the normal structure of skin, followed by descriptions of various types of skin lesions.

The skin is made up of three layers - the epidermis, dermis and hypodermis. Depending on which layer is affected, the colour and texture of the skin may look or feel different.

1.2.2. Common changes in the skin - the key skin lesion types

This booklet uses the key skin lesion types as a starting point. These include lumps, ulcers, swelling, patches, plaques, blisters and other important signs.2 They are described below, along with their subtypes or associated condition.

1.2.2.1. Lumps

Lumps are raised areas on or underneath the skin that you can see or feel. They can appear anywhere on the body. Lumps can be small or large, with a surface that feels smooth, rough or even wart-like. They may feel soft or firm to the touch. Depending on how deep they are or how they look and feel, lumps can be further grouped into the following types.

Papule: A small, solid lump on the skin. It is typically firm and raised, and may be grouped with others to form larger skin lesions.

Nodule: A lump that forms on or underneath the skin, usually larger and deeper than a papule. It is often well-defined and firm to the touch.

Tumor: A larger, solid lump that forms on or underneath the skin. It is usually firm and bigger than other lumps, though the size can vary. Tumors can be either benign (noncancerous) or malignant (cancerous).

Cyst: A closed sac located underneath the skin that contains fluid, pus, or soft material. Cysts are typically smooth, round, and firm, and may move. slightly under the skin when gently palpated. They often remain unchanged for extended periods but can become painful or swollen if infected.

1.2.2.2. Ulcers

An ulcer is a break in the skin that results in an open wound. Ulcers are often round or oval in shape, but they also have uneven or irregular edges. They typically extend deeper than the superficial layer of the skin. The base of the ulcer may appear red and raw, or it may be covered by dead tissue or a yellow surface crust. Ulcers are a common feature seen in several skin NTDs.

1.2.2.3. Swelling

Swelling, or oedema, occurs when excess fluid accumulates in tissues, leading to noticeable enlargement of the affected area. It is most easily observed in the limbs-particularly the arms or legs- where comparison between sides can be made. However, swelling can also occur on the face, scalp, or other parts of the body, especially in the presence of inflammation or infection.

Pressure on the skin leaves temporary indentation (pitting).

Swollen areas may feel firm or soft to the touch. Pressing gently but firmly with a finger may leave a temporary indentation on the skin surface (pitting oedema). Swelling can also be associated with pain (tenderness) and warmth. It is important to ask the patient about pain before examining or palpating the area.

In some cases, swelling may worsen throughout the day and improve with rest and elevation of the affected limb. However, certain types of swelling are persistent and do not fluctuate—such as those seen in conditions like mycetoma or chromoblastomycosis. In some cases, swelling may interfere with daily activities, such as wearing clothing or shoes, due to tightness or discomfort.

20.content:
1.2.2.4. Patches

A patch is a flat area of skin that looks different in colour (lighter, darker, redder, etc.) or texture, compared with the surrounding skin. It may feel smooth, dry, or rough to the touch. They may also have decreased sensation, as seen in leprosy.

1.2.2.5. Plaques

A plaque is a raised, flat-topped area of skin that may feel thickened or rough to the touch. The surface can appear dry, scaly, or crusted, and the edges may be well defined or gradually merge with the surrounding skin. Plaques can vary in size, shape, and sensation, and may be associated with a range of skin conditions, including several skin NTDs.

1.2.2.6, Blisters and pustules

Blisters and pustules are both fluid-filled bumps on the skin, but they contain different types of fluid.

Blister (vesicle or bulla): A raised lesion filled with clear or yellowish fluid. Small blisters are referred to as vesicles, while larger ones are called bullae. Blisters may result from friction, burns, infections, or various skin diseases. They are often fragile and may rupture easily, leading to open sores or crusting.

addition to the six key types of skin lesions described above, there are other skin changes that may support the identification or description of specific conditions.

Erythema: This is redness of the skin resulting from increased blood flow to the affected area. It may indicate irritation, infection, inflammation, or an allergic reaction. The affected skin may feel warm, tender, or painful to the touch.

Scales: Dry _ flakes or peeling of the outer layer of the skin (stratum corneum). They are often observed on patches or plaques and may indicate chronic inflammation, skin irritation, or the healing phase of a skin condition.

1.3. Algorithms - using key skin signs for screening and diagnosis

This section provides algorithms to support the screening and diagnosis of patients presenting with skin lesions. The algorithms are organized according to six key types of skin lesions as starting points: lumps, ulcers, swelling, patches, plaques, and blisters.

Each algorithm guides you through potential causes to helo narrow down the diagnosis and determine appropriate management.

These tools are designed to support clinical decision-making, helping you recognize conditions, identify next steps, and determine when referral is necessary:

Green indicates treatment can be ———> initiated at your level. Yellow indicates referral is recommended. ar ;

Red indicates urgent referral is needed.

Be aware of the limitation of the algorithms:

e The algorithms do not cover all diseases. If you see a condition that is not included or are uncertain about the diagnosis, refer the patient for further evaluation.

e Symptoms can fluctuate over time and may not always be consistent.

The algorithms are based on the typical presentation of each skin disease. However, some conditions may present atypically and not match the features described here. This is particularly common in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS, diabetes, or older age, who may show less typical signs. Atypical presentations are an important indication for referral and further clinical assessment.

When you should refer a patient to a hospital or to a specialist:

e When you see signs and symptoms of acute infection or inflammation;

® When you find your patient to be severely ill;

® When your patient has symptoms other than those on the skin; for example, high fever, joint pain, etc.;

® When the skin condition looks atypical;

® When you cannot make a diagnosis; and

® When your patient is not responding to treatment and not improving.

This chapter describes the major skin NTDs in the South-East Asia Region. Signs and symptoms of each disease are provided in alignment with the questions introduced in Chapter 1.

Emphasizing a skin sign and symptom-based approach, wherein the diagnosis is derived from an analysis of symptoms, this chapter underlines the importance of understanding the signs presented by patients affected by skin NTDs. 2.1.1. What is leprosy?

Leprosy, also known as Hansen’s disease, iS a chronic skin infection caused by the bacteria called Mycobacterium (M.) leprae. The disease mainly affects the skin and the peripheral nerves. In some cases, it can also affect multiple organs including the eyes and the upper respiratory tract. Leprosy can occur in people of any age, ranging from early infancy to very old age. The disease is curable and treatment in the early stages can prevent disability.

2.1.2. How is it transmitted?

Leprosy is likely transmitted via droplets from the nose and mouth during close and frequent contact with untreated cases. Even when infected, most individuals do not develop the disease as their immunity can fight the bacteria. Only those who have low or abnormal immunity against the bacteria develop the disease.

2.1.35. What are the common symptoms?

The symptoms of leprosy include those that appear on the skin and in the peripheral nerves. The incubation period (time between initial exposure to the infectious agent and development of symptoms) of leprosy can range from a few years to, sometimes, more than several decades.

How a patient manifests the disease largely depends on his/her immune response against the bacteria and this leads to a wide variety of its symptoms. Initial symptoms may go unnoticed by patients - this is common - as there can be subtle changes to the skin or because they are asymptomatic. The symptoms progress very slowly. Patients may first come to care because of leprosy reactions (see section 2.1.5.).

2.1.3.1 Symptoms of the skin

Leprosy can affect the skin in many different ways. Common signs include pale (hypopigmented) or reddish skin patch(es), as well as multiple lumps on the face and body. These skin lesions may have a dry or scaly surface. Importantly, loss of sensation or tingling sensation over the extremities is a sign of peripheral neuropathy and should raise suspicion for leprosy.

2.1.4. How is it diagnosed?

A case of leprosy is diagnosed when an individual has at least one of the three cardinal signs:

Skin lesion(s) with definite loss or decreased sensation

Thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or weakness in the muscles supplied by that nerve; and

Microscopic detection of acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear (SSS).

How to check for sensory loss in leprosy?

Loss of sensation is one of the earliest and most important signs of leprosy. A simple test can be carried out using a wisp of cotton or the rounded end of a ballpoint pen. With the patient’s eyes closed, gently touch the skin on and around any suspected patch, and ask the patient to indicate when they feel the touch. Always compare the sensation over the suspected patch with areas of normal skin. If sensation is reduced or absent on the patch, the patient should be referred for further evaluation.

Figure 2.1.9. Assessment of sensory loss in a patient with suspected leprosy.

Classification of leprosy

Leprosy can be classified into two types: paucibacillary and multibacillary. The differences in symptoms exist due to originating from the differences in patients’ immune response against M. /eprae.

The paucibacillary (PB) type is defined as a case of leprosy with 1-5 skin lesions.

The multibacillary (MB) type is defined as a case of leprosy with six or more skin lesions or with nerve involvement (pure neuritis or any number of skin lesions and neuritis) or with the demonstrated presence of bacilli in a slit-skin smear.

The treatment duration varies between the two types and therefore, it is important to differentiate the two.

Slit-skin smears are positive only in the MB type, when there are many bacteria in the skin lesions.

2.1.5. What is a leprosy reaction?

Leprosy reactions are inflammatory conditions occurring in the disease due to immune response against M. leprae, the causative bacteria. In general, immune response is a defense mechanism of the human body to attack and destroy the germ, but, in some situations, such as in leprosy reaction, it can overreact or mistakenly attack the human body parts causing inflammatory symptoms.

There are two types of leprosy reactions - type 1 reaction or reversal reaction and type 2 reaction or erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL). In type 1 reaction, the pre-existing lesions may worsen and show up as oedema and/or erythema. In type 2 reaction, patients abruptly develop new lesions, usually very painful erythematous nodules underneath the skin. They may also present with systemic symptoms, including high fever, joint pains, swelling of lymph nodes and inflammation of the eyes. In both reaction types, neuritis may occur, which may lead to lifelong nerve damage.

Self-care and rehabilitation: Tell the patient about the importance of self care for affected eyes, hands and feet, and keeping them in good condition.

e Wear soft shoes or sandals that have thick outer soles and comfortable insoles.

e Inthe morning and evening every day, examine hands and feet carefully for any wounds and early signs of muscle weakness.

e Soak hands and feet in lukewarm (not hot) water for 10-20 minutes. After soaking, rub some oil on the skin of hands and feet - for example, petroleum jelly or vegetable oils, such as palm oil, groundnut oil, coconut oil and sunflower oil.

e Protect the eyes against dust, sunlight and dryness. During the day, wear glasses, a hat or a scarf. At night, sleep under a net or a blanket and tie a cloth loosely over the eyes, if they do not close properly Clagophthalmos).

2.1.7. How can leprosy be prevented from spreading?

Leprosy is one of the least infectious diseases, with a very low risk of transmission. The most effective way to prevent the spread of leprosy is through early detection and prompt treatment of infectious cases, particularly those with multibacillary leprosy, who are known to transmit the disease. Multidrug therapy (MDT) not only cures leprosy but also interrupts its transmission.

Contact tracing is an important preventive strategy, especially in high-endemic areas, to help reduce the number of new cases in the community. WHO currently recommends that eligible individuals who are in close contact with a confirmed leprosy case may receive preventive treatment, such as single dose rifampicin, to lower their risk of developing the disease.*

Leishmaniasis is a parasitic skin infection caused by a group of protozoan parasites known as Leishmania. is transmitted by female sandflies. About 20 species of Leishmania are known to cause disease in humans.

Post kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a skin condition that can occur after treatment for visceral leishmaniasis. It appears as skin lesions and may play a role in ongoing transmission of the disease.

2.2.2. How is it transmitted?

Leishmaniasis is transmitted through the bite of female sandflies. These sandflies become infected with protozoan parasites while feeding on the blood of an infected individual and then transmit the parasites to new host (humans) during subsequent blood meals.

How do sandflies look like?

Sandflies are tiny insects around 1.5-3 mm in size. It is smaller than regular mosquitoes and can be difficult to see by the naked eye. They actively feed on blood at dawn and dusk. Sandflies live in animal burrows, caves, and in peri-domestic settings like in wall cracks.

The disease usually begins as a red papule at the site of the sandfly bite, as a single lesion, although multiple lesions can occur. Over the course of weeks to months, the papule progresses to a painless crusted nodule, plaque or ulcer, often with raised edges forming a “volcano-like” appearance.

2.3.1. What is lymphatic filariasis?

Lymphatic filariasis (LF), commonly known as elephantiasis, is caused by infection by parasitic worms known as nematodes (roundworms), including Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi and Brugia timori.

These parasites target the lymphatic system, an essential component of the body’s fluid regulation and immune function. When the lymphatic system is damaged, fluid can accumulate in various parts of the body, most commonly the legs, arms, breasts, or genitalia—leading to chronic swelling and disfigurement. Lymphatic filariasis is one of the leading causes of permanent disability globally and has significant social and economic consequences for affected individuals and communities.

2.35.2. How is it transmitted?

Lymphatic filariasis is soread from person to person by mosquitoes. Adult worms live in the human lymph nodes or vessels, where they mate and produce millions of baby worms, known as microfilariae. These microfilariae circulate in the person’s blood and are taken up by a mosquito when it bites an infected individual. Inside the mosquito, the microfilariae grow and develop into infective worms. When the mosquito bites another person, these infective worms are passed on from the mosquito to the new person. The worms live for about 5-7 years or sometimes longer. Prolonged exposure to multiple mosquito bites, spanning several months to years, is needed for lymphatic filariasis to develop.

2.35.35. What are the common symptoms?

Lymphatic filariasis often causes no symptoms in the early stages. Damage to the lymph vessels happens over time. When clinical symptoms do appear, they typically develop years after the initial infection.

The most common clinical manifestations include:

e Lymphoedema

Swelling of body parts due to fluid accumulation, most commonly affecting the legs, but also observed in the arms, breasts, or genitalia. The affected area may feel heavy, tight, or uncomfortable.

This can occur in women, although it is less common.

Patients with lymphoedema are at risk of secondary bacterial infections. Breaks in the skin may allow the entry of bacteria into the body. This can be from eczema, fungal infections between the toes, ulcers or even small injuries. These are called bacterial entry lesions and can cause recurrent infections, also known as “acute attacks” or “red legs”. Repeated attacks can lead to thickening of the skin and hardening of the limb, with secondary skin changes such as nodules and warty growths. This can progress to a condition known as elephantiasis, where the affected limb becomes enlarged and deformed.

2.3.4. How is it diagnosed?

The standard method for diagnosing active infection of lymphatic filariasis is the detection of microfilariae (larval stage of the parasite) by microscopic examination of thick blood smears (20-60 UL) obtained from a finger-prick sample. In most endemic areas of Asia, microfilariae circulate in the peripheral blood with a nocturnal periodicity (they are present in higher numbers at night), so blood collection should be done between 10:00 p.m. and 2:00 a.m. to maximize diagnostic accuracy. However, in areas where subperiodic W. bancrofti or Brugia species are endemic such as parts of Thailand and Indonesia, microfilariae may be detectable during daytime hours as well, and timing of blood collection should be adjusted accordingly.

WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (RDTSs) are available to detect circulating filarial antigens specific to Wuchereria bancrofti. A positive antigen test indicates an active or recent infection and is particularly useful in settings where microscopy is not feasible. For Brugia species, antibody-based card tests are available; however, these tests cannot distinguish between current and past infections.

As lymphoedema and other chronic manifestations of lymphatic filariasis can develop many years after the initial infection, laboratory test results may be negative in such cases. In these instances, diagnosis is made clinically, based on the presence of characteristic signs and symptoms.

2.3.5. How can lymphatic filariasis be treated and managed?

Lymphatic filariasis treatment involves two key components: (1) treatment of the underlying infection, and (2) management of long-term complications through morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP). MMDP includes lymphoedema management, treatment of acute inflammatory episodes (acute attacks), and surgical management of hydrocele.

2.3.5.1. Treating infection

Although lymphoedema is mostly irreversible, a person with a positive result of blood examination (positive microfilariae or with antigen positivity), which indicates underlying active or recent infections, and who lives in countries without onchocerciasis can be administered one of the following regimens:

® ivermectin (200 mcg/kg) together with diethylcarbamazine citrate (DEC) (6 mg/kg) and albendazole (400 mg);

® diethylcarbamazine citrate (DEC) (6 mg/kg) and albendazole (400 mg); or

® DEC 6 mg/kg alone for 12 days.

2.3.5.2. Morbidity management and disability

Lymphatic filariasis can cause long-term complications such as lymphoedema and hydrocele, which can lead to disability and significantly reduce the quality of life. Early and consistent management of these complications is essential to prevent progression. This approach is known as morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP).

MMDP includes lymphoedema management, treatment of acute attack and surgical management of hydrocele, alongside treatment for underlying filarial infection. Together, these interventions form WHO’s Essential Package of Care, which is a key pillar of the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis. This package should be delivered through the primary health care system and maintained even after national elimination targets are met, to ensure long-term care for affected individuals.

Lymphoedema management relies on a self-care programme that must be continued at home by the affected person. Health-care workers play a critical role in initiating, educating, and supporting patients to carry out this self-care regularly. Consistent practice can greatly improve quality of life and reduce complications.

Educate the patient about seeking immediate care when the affected limbs get red, swollen and/or painful (acute attack) - these are signs and symptoms of secondary infection, which needs immediate treatment with antibiotics. If you suspect this acute attack in your patient, refer them immediately to a health facility for further evaluation and care. Repeated acute attacks can lead to irreversible swelling and hardening of the skin.

2.3.5.2.3. Management of hydrocele

Hydrocele is a common clinical manifestation of lymphatic filariasis in men and is managed through surgical intervention, known as hydrocelectomy. Patients with hydrocele should be referred to a specialist or a hospital equipped with the necessary skills and facilities for safe surgical care. Proper pre-operative assessment and post-operative management are essential to reduce the risk of complications. When performed correctly, hydrocelectomy is typically a curative procedure that can significantly improve the patient’s quality of life.

2.35.6. How can lymphatic filariasis be prevented from spreading?

Not everyone bitten by an infected mosquito will develop lymphatic filariasis. While many people living in endemic areas are exposed to the parasite, only some of those infected will go on to develop symptoms. The risk is higher among individuals who do not receive preventive chemotherapy.

In these areas, mass drug administration (MDA) is conducted once a year for the entire at-risk population. The aim of MDA is to reduce the number of microfilariae (baby worms) in the blood of infected individuals, thereby interrupting transmission by mosquitoes in the community. Taking MDA medicines every year is essential to help stop the spread of the disease. In addition, it is important to avoid mosquito bites (see page 104: How to avoid mosquito bites).

2.4. Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis

Deep mycoses are fungal infections that affect the deeper layers of the skin and, in some cases, the underlying tissues. This section introduces the three major types commonly found in the WHO South-East Asia Region.

2.4.1.1. What is chromoblastomycosis?

Chromoblastomycosis is a chronic skin infection caused by certain types of fungi that produce brown pigments. These fungi are found in soil, wood and decaying plant materials, such as those from palm trees and cacti. Some of the fungi that are known to cause chromoblastomycosis include Phialophora, Fonsecaea and Cladophialophora species.

The disease primarily affects individuals with frequent exposure to soil and plant materials. It is considered an occupational disease, most commonly seen in farmers, forestry workers, animal handlers, and others engaged in outdoor manual labour.

2.4.1.2. How is it transmitted?

The fungi may enter the skin from any injuries or wounds - for example, a puncture with a splinter when walking barefoot. It does not get transmitted from human to human.

2.4.1.5. What are the common symptoms?

Usually, the lesion begins on the foot or leg, but other exposed areas of the body can also be affected. It starts as a small, singular, elevated lesion, followed by a very slow growth of tissue that produces crusted, verrucous (“warty”) or ulcerated lesions. New lesions may develop at times as satellites around the initial lesion. Without treatment, the lesion will worsen and grow, and more lesions can appear in other places. These lesions can be warty, tumor-like or form open wounds.

Itching is usually present, which is believed to contribute to the spread of the infection through scratching and auto-inoculating (or “self-implanting”) the infection. Sometimes, it can also be painful. With time, as the severity increases, oedema and secondary infection may result in daily activities getting affected. Squamous cell carcinoma (a malignant tumor of the skin) may arise from chronic lesions.

2.4.1.4. How is it diagnosed?

Chromoblastomycosis can be diagnosed by identifying the fungi from skin scrapings or skin biopsy. The best samples for these tests are the lesions with small black dots (“cayenne pepper” appearance). Dermoscopy, an examination of skin lesions with a special magnifying camera for the skin, can help visualize these dots to assist in selecting the best sites for sample collection. Alternatively, the photo enlargement function of smartphones can sometimes be used, if no special equipment is available.

Under the microscope, the fungus appears as thick-walled, large, round cells, dark brown in colour. The dark brown colour is from the melanin pigment in the walls of the organism.

If available, a sample can be sent to a laboratory for fungal culture under special conditions. When the culture is positive, additional tests, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and DNA sequencing, may be used to identify the causative species. However, accurately identifying the specific fungus can be challenging.

2.4.2.1. What is mycetoma?

Mycetoma is a chronic skin infection that can be caused by certain types of fungi or, in some cases, by bacteria. The fungal form is known as eumycetoma, while the bacterial form is called actinomycetoma. Both forms produce similar signs and symptoms and are often grouped together due to their overlapping clinical presentation and shared treatment challenges.

Mycetoma is commonly found in individuals who walk barefoot or have frequent contact with soil, wood, or plant materials, particularly in rural and agricultural settings. It occurs most often in tropical and subtropical areas where short rainy seasons followed by long dry seasons favour the growth of thorny vegetation. In many affected regions, it is considered an occupational disease.

2.4.2.2. How is it transmitted?

Like chromoblastomycosis, the fungi and bacteria that cause mycetoma are found in soil, wood, and plant materials. Infection typically occurs when these organisms enter the body through minor skin injuries, such as thorn pricks, cuts, or splinters.

2.4.2.5. What are the common symptoms?

Mycetoma often begins as firm, painless nodules or a swelling beneath the skin. The swelling may feel “woody”’—meaning it is hard, thick, and not soft to the touch, resembling the texture of dry wood. Although it commonly affects the foot, it can develop on any part of the body. Over time, these lesions may enlarge, form oozing sores or sinuses, and impair the function of the affected limb, making it difficult to bear weight. A sinus iS a small tunnel or channel that drains pus, debris, or infected material from the affected area through an opening in the skin. The pus discharged from a mycetoma sinus may contain small, distinct particles known as “grains,” which are a characteristic feature of the disease.

The classic triad of clinical features of mycetoma includes:

v A) R °o Painless, firm Multiple sinus Discharge containing subcutaneous swelling; formations; and pus and “grains”.

If left untreated, the infection can spread to other parts of the body. In the long term, it can destroy the underlying muscle and bone.

2.4.2.4. How is it diagnosed?

The causative pathogen, whether it is a fungus or a bacterium, can be identified through direct or microscopic observation of a grain. Samples can be taken from the discharging fluids, scrapings of sinus walls and skin biopsies. Saline dressing applied overnight over the lesion or aspiration of grains from an unopened sinus tract can be also used.

While culture is not essential for diagnosis, it can aid in identifying the causative species when available. The choice of culture media depends on whether a fungal or bacterial infection is suspected. If the culture is positive, further identification can be carried out using advanced techniques such as PCR and DNA sequencing, although these are not widely accessible. Accurate identification is often challenging due to the wide variety of organisms that can cause mycetoma.

Where available, imaging techniques such as ultrasound, X-ray, computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are valuable for assessing the depth and extent of the disease—especially in cases where infection has spread to muscles or bones.

2.4.3.1. What is sporotrichosis?

Sporotrichosis is a chronic skin infection caused by a fungus called Sporothrix schenckii. This fungus is commonly found on rose thorns, hay, sohagnum moss, twigs, and in soil. Because of its association with gardening and plant materials, the disease is often referred to as “rose gardener’s disease.”

2.4.3.2. How is it transmitted?

Like chromoblastomycosis and mycetoma, sporotrichosis is an environmentally acquired infection. It is commonly seen in gardeners, forestry workers, and farmers. The fungus enters the skin through small cuts or puncture wounds that occur during contact with contaminated plant material or soil.

2.4.3.5. What are the common symptoms?

Sporotrichosis typically begins as a small, painless red nodule at the site where the fungus enters the skin. The infection often spreads along the lymphatic channels of the limb, resulting in a line of similar lesions—a pattern known as “linear” distribution. Over time, these nodules may ulcerate and begin to drain fluid or pus.

In rare cases, particularly in individuals with weakened immune systems, the infection can spread beyond the skin to affect the lungs, bones, joints, or nervous system.

2.5.1. What is scabies?

Scabies is a skin disease caused by a mite of about 0.4 mm in size (about the tip of a pen). Only female mites infest humans. They burrow into the skin to lay eggs, leading to allergic reactions that cause intense itching and skin lesions. If left untreated, the mites can survive on the skin for several months. Even after successful treatment, itching may persist for some time due to the body’s continued immune response.

Scabies is a common condition that can affect people of all ages. It spreads easily in close-contact settings such as households, schools, and childcare centres. Outbreaks are more likely in crowded environments with limited hygiene access, including refugee camps, prisons, and institutional facilities.

Figure 2.5.1. Scabies mite

2.5.2. How is it transmitted?

Scabies is primarily transmitted through prolonged, direct skin-to-skin contact, for example, between spouses, parents and children, or other close household members. Sexual contact is also a common mode of transmission. Brief or casual contact, such as a handshake or light touch, is unlikely to soread the disease.

Indirect transmission through infested clothing, bedding, or towels is uncommon but possible, especially in cases of crusted scabies, where the mite burden is much higher and shedding of mites onto surfaces is more extensive.

2.5.3. What are the common symptoms?

After the initial exposure to scabies, it can take up to six weeks for symptoms to appear. However, in individuals who have had scabies before, symptoms may develop much more quickly.

The symptoms are caused by an allergic reaction to the mites, leading to intense itching and a rash that can appear anywhere on the body. In older children and adults, the skin above the neck is usually not affected. Common skin lesions include papules, nodules, and scaling. Burrows—thin, thread-like lines caused by the mites, are typically found in the web spaces between the fingers, on the palms, and around the wrists.

Persistent scratching can break the skin, increasing the risk of secondary bacterial infections, most commonly impetigo (see Section 3.2.1). If left untreated, such infections may lead to serious complications, including post streptococcal conditions that can affect the heart and kidneys.

Scabies should be suspected in patients presenting with a new, widespread, and intensely itchy rash, particularly when there is a history of close contact with others who have similar symptoms. In most cases, a clinical diagnosis is sufficient, based on the characteristic appearance and distribution of lesions, along with nocturnal itching.

If available, dermoscopy or microscopic examination of skin scrapings can help confirm the diagnosis by identifying mites, eggs, or faecal pellets.

2.5.5. What is crusted scabies?

Crusted scabies, also known as Norwegian scabies, is a highly contagious and severe form of scabies. It occurs when an individual is infested with thousands to millions of mites, typically due to weakened immunity.

Affected individuals develop thick, scaly, crusted plaques that can appear anywhere on the body, but are often most prominent between the fingers, wrists, armpits, nipples, male genitalia, waist, and buttocks. Unlike common scabies, itching may be absent or minimal, which can delay diagnosis and increase the risk of transmission.

2.6.1. What is yaws?

Yaws is a chronic skin infection caused by spiral bacteria called Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue. The bacteria that causes yaws is genetically closely related to syphilis. However, unlike syphilis, yaws is not sexually transmitted.

Almost all cases of yaws occur in children under 15 years of age, with the peak incidence in 6-10 years. The disease mainly affects the skin and if left untreated, can also affect the cartilages and bones.

Yaws is curable with one-dose of oral azithromycin; treatment in the early stages can prevent long-term disability.

2.6.2. How is it transmitted?

The transmission of yaws is known to occur from skin-to-skin contact with another person who has yaws lesions on the skin through a break (cut or wound) in the skin. The bacteria that cause yaws only infect humans. The incubation period spans 9-90 days, with an average of 21 days. Poverty and poor water, sanitation and personal hygiene facilitate the spread of yaws.

2.6.3 What are the common symptoms?

The clinical course of yaws is grouped into three stages.

e Primary yaws...

Yaws first presents as a papilloma, which is an outward-growing lump that has a bumpy or warty surface. This initial lesion is known as the “mother yaw”, which develops at the site where the bacteria entered the body Cinoculation). Without treatment, the papilloma can ulcerate, often with a red base and raised edges.

2.6.4. How is it diagnosed?

Diagnosis is primarily based on the clinical appearance of skin lesions and supported by serological testing. Once lesions ulcerate, they may resemble other skin conditions, making diagnosis more difficult. Therefore, laboratory confirmation, such as the use of a rapid diagnostic test (RDT), is recommended to support the clinical assessment.

In field settings, yaws can be confirmed using a rapid diagnostic test called the Dual Path Platform (DPP® Syphilis Screen and Confirm Assay). This test is also used for syphilis; unfortunately, the test cannot distinguish yaws from syphilis. Therefore, the interpretation of results from this test, with regard to adults who live in yaws-endemic areas, needs careful clinical assessment. The DPP test can indicate whether a person has had past or current active yaws infection. It is important to distinguish between these two because someone with a past infection will not be in need of treatment or transmit the disease, whereas someone with an active infection will be in need of treatment and can transmit the disease.

About 40% of ulcers clinically misidentified as yaws are known to be caused by other bacteria, the major one of which is Haemophilus ducreyi. This is also why it is important to perform a diagnostic test.

2.6.6. How can yaws be prevented from spreading?

There is no vaccine for yaws. Prevention focuses on early detection and treatment.

The present yaws eradication strategy recommended by WHO includes providing a single dose of azithromycin during total community treatment (TCT) for all individuals residing in yaws-endemic areas. Box: Buruli ulcer

What is Buruli ulcer?

Buruli ulcer is one of the skin-related neglected tropical diseases (skin NTDs), caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans—a bacterium that produces a toxin (mycolactone) which damages the skin and soft tissue. The disease often begins as a painless swelling or nodule, usually on the limbs, and may progress into a large ulcer with undermined edges and significant skin loss if left untreated. Despite the severity of the lesions, pain is often minimal, which may delay diagnosis.

Buruli ulcer is most commonly reported in parts of West and Central Africa, but cases have also been identified in other regions, including Australia, South America, and Japan. The exact mode of transmission remains unclear, though contact with contaminated environments is believed to play a role.

While no confirmed cases have been detected in the WHO South-East Asia Region, under -recognized or misdiagnosed cases may exist. Health workers should be aware of this condition and consider it in the differential diagnosis of chronic or atypical skin ulcers.

If Buruli ulcer is suspected, a skin biopsy should be taken. Histopathological examination can support the diagnosis. Samples must be carefully stored and sent to one of the WHO Skin NTD Laboratory Network (LABNET) facilities for PCR confirmation.

The list of designated LABNET facilities is available here:

This chapter introduces some of the most common skin diseases encountered in communities across the WHO South-East Asia Region. Conditions are organized by their origin and pathogenesis, with key clinical features highlighted to help you recognize signs and symptoms. Because many skin diseases share similar treatment approaches, general management guidance is provided at the end of each section. Always follow national or regional treatment protocols when available.

Thinking through differential diagnoses is a critical step in reaching an accurate diagnosis. Even if a skin lesion looks familiar, always ask yourself: “What e/se could this be?”

Developing a list of possible diagnoses based on observed signs and symptoms takes both experience and knowledge. This chapter aims to expand your understanding of a broad range of skin conditions and sharpen your ability to distinguish between them. Revisit the clinical images and reflect on what makes one condition different from another.

If a diagnosis is unclear, or if the patient presents with a chronic, treatment-resistant, or severe condition, refer the patient to a specialist for further evaluation.

A Emerging threats: Drug-resistant fungi

The incidence and prevalence of drug resistant fungi is on the rise!! Especially, pathogenic dermatophytes resistant to terbinafine are widespread not only in the South-East Asian region where it originated but spreading rapidly throughout the world. Major factors for the develooment of anti-fungal resistance is attributed to the widespread and indiscriminate use of broadspectrum antifungals in both medicine and agriculture, as well as inadequate adherence to hygienic practices. There are actions that we can take at an individual level to mitigate this emergence. It is important that you make efforts to restrict inappropriate anti-fungal medication usage by limiting unnecessary prescriptions and educating your patients on their usage. You can also educate your patients and community members in hygienic practices to cut the infection chain.

Wounds are common, especially in remote communities. They may result from a variety of causes, such as injury, burns, infections, or underlying medical conditions, but regardless of the cause, the basic principles of wound care remain the same. Proper wound care is essential to prevent infection, support healing, and reduce the risk of long-term complications such as scarring or disability.

This chapter begins with the fundamentals of wound care, followed by guidance on assessing the cause of wounds and additional tips to promote healing. Wound care techniques can be taught to patients and their families, so that care can continue where they live.

You can also refer to ANNEXURE 5 where it provides a flow chart to help guide wound care.

4.1. Basics of wound care

There are five main principles to support and accelerate the wound healing process.

Diagnose and treat . . 1 Wash the wound infection early Remove dead skin, tissues . . ——~ 2. Keep the wound moist and any foreign objects ra P

Timely dressing change

1. Wash the wound

Keep the wound and surrounding skin clean by washing with clean water or a saline solution. Wash gently. This is to wash away any bacteria or debris from the surface of the wound. Avoid using hydrogen peroxide, alcohol or iodine products. These products may damage the newly growing cells to heal the wound. It is also important to wear gloves, but if they are not available, wash your hands very well with soap and water before and after touching the wound.

If you are worried that the water may not be clean, boil the water. Cool it down before using it on the wound. Clean water means that it should be fit for drinking.

2. Keep the wound moist

The wound should not be too dry or too moist. As it is also composed of living cells such as those in any other parts of our body, it needs some moisture for the new skin tissue to grow and close the wound. A moist wound environment is not only good for wound healing, but it also helps in relieving pain.

If the wound surface is dry, an ointment can be applied. Petroleum jelly is one of the best and inexpensive ointments to apply on a wound. However, it may not always be available. Other products or natural sources Choney, turmeric, aloe vera, etc.) can be used in community settings as alternatives. If you are unsure about what you have is appropriate for application on a wound, consult a specialist.

Chapter 4: Managing wounds

3. Timely dressing change

Wound dressings help maintain a moist environment at the wound surface, which supports healing. Use clean gauze or cloth to cover the wound. The frequency of dressing changes depends on the wound condition and the type of dressing used. In general, dressings should be changed once a day or whenever they become wet or dirty.

If

the wound produces excessive exudate - moisture that leaks onto the surrounding skin and causes maceration - the dressing should be changed more frequently. For clean wounds that are healing well, less frequent dressing changes (such as a few times per week) may be sufficient.

Maceration

For effective wound healing, the skin around the wound (called the periwound area) must remain healthy. Excessive exudate (fluid) from the wound can damage this surrounding skin. Maceration happens when too much exudate makes the nearby skin look whitish, soft, or soggy. This is a sign that the dressing may need to be changed more often to protect the skin and support proper healing.

4. Remove dead skin and tissues and any foreign objects

Dead skin and tissues must be removed to support healing - this process is called ‘debridement’. Debridement can be done surgically in a sterile way with sterile sharp instruments or, if available, chemically with ointments which help dissolve dead tissues. If bone is exposed or can be felt, this is a strong indication of possible osteomyelitis (bone infection) and the patient should be referred to a specialist for further evaluation and possible removal.

Any foreign objects, such as nails, small stones, or wood splinters, can also interfere with wound healing and must be removed. People affected by leprosy or diabetes, who often have reduced sensation, may not feel pain and therefore may not notice these objects.

5. Diagnose and treat infection early

Infection can delay wound healing. Not only it may make wound healing stagnant, it may even worsen the wound, leading to a longer time to heal. It is therefore important to diagnose and treat infection as early as possible.

A wound may be infected if:

e@ it becomes red, swollen, hot, and painful;

The infection may be spreading to other parts of the body if:

@ the patient has a fever;

e lymph nodes (felt as lumps in the neck, armpits, or groin) become swollen and tender.

In such cases, treat the patient with systemic antibiotics. Wash the wound thoroughly with clean water and increase the frequency of dressing changes.

When a patient is experiencing fever and chills, suspect sepsis, which is a serious condition that the body is over reacting and causing extreme response to the infection. The patient may also present with altered mental status or low blood pressure (hypotension). Refer the patient immediately to a doctor.

110.sectionTitle: Assess and correct cause(s) of wound
110.content:
4.2. Assess and correct cause(s) of wound

Assessing and treating the underlying disease or condition are crucial for providing patients with the right care. Wounds can occur due to various causes, ranging from trauma and burns (external causes) to infectious to non-infectious ones (internal causes).

If it is an internal cause, treatment and management of the cause are as important as wound care to achieve complete healing. If these causes are not managed well, it can lead to delayed wound healing. For example, if you do not manage the blood sugar level in a patient with diabetic foot ulcer, the wound will likely lead to a long healing course. If you see a patient with a wound from skin tuberculosis, you need to treat for tuberculosis, only then the wound will heal.

Certain external factors can delay wound healing. For example, pressure ulcers require relief of pressure at the wound site through frequent position changes. This is especially important for people with diabetes or leprosy, who often have reduced sensation in their limbs.

Without normal sensation, pressure may be unevenly distributed, particularly on the soles of the feet, resulting in wounds. In such cases, off-loading devices such as specially designed shoes or supports are needed to reduce pressure on specific areas and allow the wound to heal.

Manage swelling... Swelling (oedema) can slow down wound healing. For wounds on the lower limbs, encourage patients to elevate the affected limb to reduce swelling. Compression bandaging and gentle massage may also support the reduction of oedema and promote faster healing.

Prevent or treat physical sequelae/disability... \Wound care should aim not only for wound closure, but also for the preservation of physical function. Patients should not be discouraged from moving the body part affected by a wound. Instead, encourage early and safe movement from the beginning of treatment. Prolonged immobility can lead to muscle wasting and loss of strength, making it harder for patients to regain movement even after the wound has healed.

Advise and provide appropriate mobility aids such as crutches, walkers, or adaptive equipment, and teach both patients and caregivers how to use them safely. Tailor these strategies to the available resources and cultural context of the community.

Incorporating these approaches during wound care is vital to preventing physical disabilities and helping patients maintain independence and quality of life.

Eating healthy... Good nutrition is essential for wound healing. Ensure the patient is eating a balanced diet with adequate protein, fruits, and vegetables to support tissue repair and recovery.

Continue care after wound closure... Even after the wound has healed, care must continue. A scarred area remains vulnerable to breakdown or recurrence of a wound. To keep the skin healthy, apply petroleum jelly or moisturizing cream regularly to keep the skin soft and hydrated. Also avoid putting pressure on the scar area whenever possible.

Healthy skin is everyone’s right - free from diseased skin. While some skin conditions, such as atopic dermatitis, are unavoidable due to genetic predisposition, others, like injuries or infections, may result from environmental factors such as climate, overcrowding, or poor living conditions. These challenges are often difficult to overcome quickly.

However, many skin diseases can be prevented or better controlled through community-level actions. Education and awareness play a crucial role. Because skin diseases are often visible, people affected may face stigma and discrimination, which can harm both their physical and mental health. With the right knowledge and support, communities can challenge misconceptions and promote inclusion.

5.2. Protection from the sun

The sun’s ultraviolet (UV) rays can damage the skin over time, leading to sunburn, premature aging, and an increased risk of skin cancers, including melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma. Protecting the skin from the sun is therefore an important part of maintaining long-term skin health.

Simple steps to protect the skin from sun damage:

e Apply sunscreen before going outdoors, especially exposed areas like the face, arms, and legs.

e Wear sun-protective clothing, such as hats or long-sleeved shirts.

e Limit time in direct sunlight by avoiding outdoor activities during peak sunlight hours (10 a.m. to 4 p.m.), and seek shade whenever possible.

It is very important to share these tips with anyone who spends a significant amount of time in the sun, including agricultural workers and fishermen.

5.3. Protection from insect bites

Preventing insect bites is an important prevention method not only for avoiding discomfort, but also for protecting oneself from getting infected with diseases spread by insects or for reducing the risk of allergic reactions.

Be cautious about the following insects:

Mosquitoes

Ticks

Mosquito bites can cause itching and discomfort. Inthe South-East Asia Region, Aedes, Anopheles and Culex mosquitoes are common. They can transmit diseases such as malaria, lymphatic filariasis, dengue, chikugunya, Zika virus and Japanese encephalitis.

Ticks are small arthropods that attach to human skin and feed on blood. Their bites are usually painless and often go unnoticed, increasing the risk of disease transmission. In this region, ticks can transmit: Indian tick typhus, scrub typhus, Kyasanur Forest Disease, and other bacterial or viral diseases.

Fleas

Sandflies

Flea bites are itchy and irritating, and in some cases, they may transmit diseases such as murine typhus and, in rare cases, plague.

Sandfly bites can be painful or itchy, and they are responsible for transmitting leishmaniasis.

5.4. Seeking care at an early stage

Encouraging patients to check their skin

“Look, ask and feel” is not only a helpful tool for a provider when assessing skin lesions, but it is also something that patients can adopt for protecting themselves. Encourage patients to look at their skin often for any new or rapidly changing lesions. Further, if there are any lesions or areas that are hard to be looked at by the patients themselves (such as their back), have them ask a trusted family member or a friend to take a closer look. Finally, encourage them to feel the lesion for an irregular or raised texture. If it does feel irregular or raised, the patients should seek medical care.

Keeping first-aid supplies at home

Keep first-aid supplies, such as plasters and dressings, readily available at home. This can prevent exposing the wound to dirt and germs at the earliest to stall secondary infections.

More awareness and seeking care at an early stage

Skin lesions are sO common in the community that many people neglect the conditions. They may think these are “a part of their lives”; they do not think that this is something for which they should seek care or which can be treated. This can lead to delays in treatment and serious complications. There needs to be a higher level of awareness about skin infections so that people will seek earlier care. Similarly, there is lack of awareness about the fact that many of these conditions can be prevented by maintaining good skin hygiene and taking care of any known wounds. Assess your community’s awareness of skin hygiene and educate.

5.5. Approaches to reducing stigma and discrimination

Many skin diseases, particularly when they affect visible parts of the body, can lead to stigma and discrimination. This is especially true for skin NTDs, such as leprosy, which have been among the most stigmatized conditions. However, many other skin diseases face similar challenges.

Stigma and discrimination, often rooted within the community, are driven by misconceptions, fear of contagion and social prejudices. In some cases, stigma may lead to isolation, affecting not only patients but also their families. Self-stigma, wherein an individual internalizes the negative attitudes of others, can be especially harmful, as it impacts the patient’s mental well-being and reduces his/her willingness to seek care.

You play a pivotal role in combating stigma as a health-care provider. It is important that you treat patients with skin NTDs and other skin conditions with dignity and respect, ensuring that your own attitudes do not contribute to the stigma. By demonstrating empathy and professionalism, you can set an example for others in the community.

Awareness campaigns

Community-based sensitization programmes, using local languages and culturally appropriate messaging, can demystify skin conditions and highlight the fact that many are curable or manageable.

Social and economic rehabilitation programmes

It is important to provide social and economic support for persons affected by skin NTDs and other stigmatized skin conditions or connect them to these services, if available. Access to vocational training and job placement programmes can help patients regain financial independence, reducing the stigma associated with being seen as dependent or incapable.

Counselling and psychosocial support

Psychological counselling and support networks play a critical role in helping individuals cope with the emotional and social impact of stigma. Establishing peer support groups where patients can share their experiences and support each other can reduce isolation and promote resilience. These groups can also serve as platforms for empowerment and advocacy.

5.6. Empowering patients to take action

AS providers, it is essential to encourage patients to take action and care for themselves, as self-care is a big part of good skin health.

Share these five key goals with your patients and answer any questions that they may have with regard to achieving these goals:

Prove to others that you are able to take care of your skin: Ensure that patients have a solid understanding of good skin hygiene.

Prove to others that you are able to prevent disability: It is important that patients know and use preventive techniques (such as wearing protective shoes, applying sunscreen and performing wound care), and prioritize including these steps in their daily lives to maintain good skin health.

Prove that you can make your life a good example for others to follow: By adopting these practices, patients can become a steward and encourage others to also follow these steps.

Find ways to help other people: Completing skin checks, encouraging good skin hygiene practices and helping others to treat their wounds can be some of the ways in which patients can help their community members. With this united effort, patients can support one another and the efforts of promoting skin health grow stronger. Additionally, patients can also become community advocates for promoting policy changes and expansion of public health efforts.

At all times, remember that you are special: Living with a skin disease can take a great mental toll, especially for diseases that carry stigma in the community. Encouraging love for self is fundamental to the success of skin disease treatment.

Conclusion

This booklet adopts a skin sign and symptom-based approach to skin NTDs and other skin diseases, moving beyond the traditional disease-specific focus, often found in previous training materials. By emphasizing the recognition of the syndromes and patterns instead of just individual diseases, this approach is designed to better align with your day-to-day clinical practice, helping you to identify and manage a broad range of skin conditions.

For any disease control efforts to be successful, community engagement is vital. Because most skin diseases do not cause immediate death, they are often overlooked by communities. Sensitization to improving the skin health of the community is crucial. As a front-line health-care worker, you are at the forefront of this effort to bring about a positive change. Your role goes beyond diagnosing and treating patients with skin diseases - you have a unique opportunity to motivate, educate and engage your community in preventing skin diseases and promoting early access to care.

If the health-seeking behaviour is such that an individual accesses health-care facilities when he/she first notices his/her abnormal skin condition, there will be fewer delays in diagnosis and treatment of skin NTDs and other debilitating skin diseases. The skin, too frequently overlooked, is an important indicator of overall health and maintaining healthy skin contributes to the well-being of the entire community.

As you continue your essential work, this booklet is intended to be a practical resource to support you in improving skin health in your communities. We hope it equips you with the knowledge and confidence needed to manage skin NTDs and other skin diseases effectively, thereby helping reduce the burden of skin diseases in the regions where you serve.

32.sectionTitle: Algorithms - using key skin signs for screening and diagnosis
32.chapterTitle: Basics of seeing a patient with skin lesions
32.content:
# Chapter 1 ASK/LOOK/FEEL algorithm: Plaques

Color legend: green = treat_locally, yellow = refer, red = urgent_referral (warning icon).

- ASK: Pain
  - Acute
    - (Known leprosy)* [*Painful plaques can be the first symptom leading to diagnosis of the disease.]
      - LOOK: Red, shiny
        - FEEL: Warm to touch, tender
          - OTHER: Peripheral nerve enlargement; reduced sensation / deformities of hands and feet
            - **Leprosy reaction** -- "Refer" -- urgency: refer
- ASK: Itch
  - Chronic
    - LOOK: Scaly or flaky surface (shared parent for next 4 columns)
      - Well-defined red lesions with silvery scales
        - FEEL: Fine scales at the margins
          - OTHER: Nail pitting; joint pain
            - **Psoriasis** -- "Refer" -- urgency: refer
      - Ring-shaped lesions; any parts of the body
        - (fine scales at margins implied)
          - **'Ringworm' / Tinea** -- "Treat" -- urgency: treat_locally
      - Ill-defined lesions; often over scalp and/or face
        - FEEL: Greasy scales
          - OTHER: Severe in patients with immunosuppression
            - **Seborrheic dermatitis** -- "Treat" -- urgency: treat_locally
      - Red, dry plaques; any parts of the body
        - FEEL: Rough skin surface
          - **Eczema** -- "Refer" -- urgency: refer
- ASK: No pain / itch
  - Chronic
    - LOOK: Hypopigmented patch(es); often on the face
      - FEEL: Intact sensation
        - OTHER: History of visceral leishmaniasis (not always obvious)
          - **PKDL** -- "Refer" -- urgency: refer
    - LOOK: Hypopigmented patch(es)
      - FEEL: Reduced sensation on the patch(es)
        - OTHER: Peripheral nerve enlargement; reduced sensation / deformities of hands and feet
          - **Leprosy** -- "Refer" -- urgency: refer

Source: Chapter 1: Basics of seeing a patient with skin lesions > Plaques (pages 32-33)

34.sectionTitle: Algorithms - using key skin signs for screening and diagnosis
34.chapterTitle: Basics of seeing a patient with skin lesions
34.content:
# Chapter 1 ASK/LOOK/FEEL algorithm: Blisters and pustules

Color legend: green = treat_locally, yellow = refer, red = urgent_referral (warning icon).

- ASK: Pain
  - Acute
    - LOOK: Multiple blisters with diffuse redness; mucosa (eyes, mouth, or genitals) may be involved
      - FEEL: Warm to touch, tender
        - OTHER: History of intake of new medication(s)
          - **Acute drug reaction** -- "Treat or refer" -- urgency: urgent_referral
    - LOOK: Unilateral, single stripe of blisters; redness
      - OTHER: Pain over the lesion, can remain after healing of skin lesions
        - **Shingles** -- "Refer" -- urgency: refer
    - LOOK: Localized around the mouth
      - OTHER: Recurrent
        - **Mouth herpes** -- "Refer" -- urgency: refer
- ASK: Itch
  - Acute
    - LOOK: Any body parts including the mouth
      - OTHER: Fever, sore throat may be present
        - **Chickenpox** -- "Treat" -- urgency: treat_locally
    - LOOK: Localized, mostly on the face, "honey-colored" crust
      - OTHER: In children
        - **Impetigo** -- "Treat" -- urgency: treat_locally
    - LOOK: Localized, multiple blisters with associated redness
      - FEEL: Warm to touch
        - OTHER: Trigger may be present
          - **Severe acute eczema** -- "Treat" -- urgency: treat_locally
- ASK: No pain / itch
  - Chronic
    - LOOK: On the extremities, mostly on the foot; no swelling
      - OTHER: Known diabetes or leprosy
        - **Diabetic bullae / Bullae from leprosy neuropathy** -- "Refer" -- urgency: refer
    - LOOK: Occurs on swelling over the extremities
      - OTHER: Known causes of swelling
        - **Edema blister / Stasis blister** -- "Treat" -- urgency: treat_locally

Source: Chapter 1: Basics of seeing a patient with skin lesions > Blisters and pustules (pages 34-35)

# Figure 2.1.8. Flow chart for diagnosing a patient with leprosy

Note: this chart is a diagnostic classification tree, not a treat/refer/urgent-referral triage chart -- the WHO green/yellow/red color legend used in the Chapter 1 ASK/LOOK/FEEL charts does NOT apply here. Boxes below use the chart's own neutral styling; urgency tags are omitted where the source doesn't provide them.

IF skin lesion(s) suggestive of leprosy = Yes:
  THEN check for peripheral nerve damage via three tests, each shown with a reference photo:
    - Sensory testing (photo: examiner testing sensation on a patient's shoulder with a fine instrument)
    - Enlargement of nerves (photo: close-up of skin over a nerve, arrows pointing to a palpable enlarged nerve cord)
    - Motor testing (photo: examiner assessing grip/motor function of the patient's hands)
  IF peripheral nerve damage present = Yes (*not all symptoms of peripheral nerve damage need to be present):
    THEN DIAGNOSE: Leprosy
    Two parallel classification pathways from this diagnosis:
      1. WHEN SLIT-SKIN SMEARS ARE NOT AVAILABLE OR DEPENDABLE -- CLASSIFY (CLINICALLY):
         - IF up to 5 skin lesions THEN PB leprosy (paucibacillary)
         - IF more than 5 skin lesions THEN MB leprosy (multibacillary)
      2. WHEN SLIT-SKIN SMEARS ARE AVAILABLE AND DEPENDABLE -- CLASSIFY (BACTERIOLOGICALLY):
         - IF smear negative (-) THEN PB leprosy
         - IF smear positive (+) THEN MB leprosy

Footnotes in original:
- "For instances where leprosy is suspected but symptoms are not strong enough to confirm diagnosis, ensure a follow-up check at 3-4 months."
- "Modified from: A new atlas of leprosy"

Source: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region > 2.1 Leprosy > Figure 2.1.8 (page 43)

55.content:
# Figure 2.2.7. Flow chart for diagnosing a patient with PKDL

Note: this is a Yes/No binary decision tree (blue diamond = Yes path, red diamond = No path), not a green/yellow/red triage chart -- the Chapter 1 traffic-light legend does not apply here. Terminal outcomes are either "Treatment for PKDL" or a differential-diagnosis referral, as shown below.

IF appearance of papules, nodules, and plaques, macular hypopigmentation = Yes:
  THEN check: lived in or travelled to VL (visceral leishmaniasis) endemic area, and/or past history of VL treatment
  IF (either of the above) = Yes:
    THEN check: loss of skin sensation?
      IF loss of skin sensation = Yes: THEN consider differential diagnosis of leprosy [branch ends here]
      IF loss of skin sensation = No:
        THEN check: rK39 rapid diagnostic test positivity
          IF rK39 positive = Yes: THEN Treatment for PKDL
          IF rK39 positive = No (or not done):
            THEN check: history of VL and/or clinical suspicion is strong?
              IF No: THEN consider other differential diagnosis [branch ends here]
              IF Yes:
                THEN check: skin slit microscopy or antigen detection test positive (+)?
                  IF Yes: THEN Treatment for PKDL
                  IF No:
                    THEN check: histopathology or molecular test positive (+)?
                      IF Yes: THEN Treatment for PKDL
                      IF No:
                        THEN check: clinical opinion by expert for differential diagnosis?
                          IF Yes: THEN Treatment for PKDL

Source: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region > 2.2 Leishmaniasis > Figure 2.2.7 (page 55)

# Annexure 5: Wound care and monitoring for simple and complicated ulcers

Note: this is a wound-management workflow, not a green/yellow/red triage chart -- no WHO traffic-light color coding is used on this page. Outcome/action boxes are used as the terminal labels instead.

Start: Wound Assessment
  Branch A -- IF simple ulcer (clean, red color; clear discharge; superficial):
    THEN follow the basics of wound care: wash the wound; keep the wound moist; timely dressing change; remove dead skin and tissues and any foreign objects (nails, stones, wood splinter)
    THEN educate patient and family on self-care
    THEN follow-up every 1-2 weeks, checking: wound surface area is smaller; less discharge; new skin is growing around the wound edges (*keep records of sizes, and if possible, take photos)
      IF signs of complicated ulcers appear during follow-up: THEN refer to doctor (re-route to Branch B below)
      IF no change in 4-6 weeks: THEN refer to doctor (re-route to Branch B below)
      IF improving as expected: THEN continue until complete closure / epithelization; if any scar, educate patient on scar management
  Branch B -- IF complicated ulcer (any one or more of: deep; discharge pus; bad smell; area around the wound is hot, red and swollen; pain; fever, chills):
    THEN refer to doctor
  Branch C -- IF any suspected underlying condition from internal causes:
    THEN refer to doctor (see internal-cause examples below)

Examples of internal causes of wounds (reference box):
  Infections: severe bacterial infection; leprosy; tuberculosis; other mycobacterial diseases; lymphatic filariasis
  Non-infections: diabetic foot; venous (stasis) ulcer; arterial (ischemic) ulcer; cutaneous tumor

Source: Annexure 5: Wound care and monitoring for simple and complicated ulcers (page 136)
